w: What's tested The white cells: "what you need to remember with white blood cells is we've got two classes and 5 types," the granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) and the agranulocytes (monocytes, lymphocytes), with each one's share, look and job; and "platelets arise from megakaryocytes. That's just knowledge you should know" B, T and NK cells: "when you hear the word humoral, think B-cell response"; the plasma cell ("associate that with antibody production and release"); helper (CD4) and cytotoxic (CD8) T cells, which read antigen on MHC; and NK cells, with no B or T markers, CD16 and ADCC, and his schematic of how MHC class I holds them back Innate versus adaptive immunity, and what belongs to each Primary versus secondary lymphoid organs: "the thymus and the bone marrow for our class" (GALT is not primary), "bone marrow, B cells, thymus, T cells," and the stroma: "epithelioreticular cells, you should associate that with the thymus" The thymus (cortex and medulla, involution to fat, 95 to 99 percent of thymocytes selected out, the blood-thymus barrier, thymic education) and the lymph node (the sinuses the lymph runs through, and where B and T cells are activated, multiply and make antibody) The spleen: "the main thing is just to really associate this PALS with the spleen," the T cell sheath around the central artery; the white and red pulp, the marginal zone and the splenic sinuses What he said won't be asked: stained images ("I'm not gonna ask you any questions specifically on stained images") and the typical concentration of each cell Dr. Herr, the course director, gave Lecture 19, Introduction to Hematology, on Tuesday, November 17, at 1 pm: a short lecture, about 37 minutes, just before Dr. Borak's Lecture 20. He opened by saying the class had seen some of this before, so "it's just a matter of jogging your memory." His deck opens the hematology block in two halves: the cells of the blood and what each one does, then the lymphoid organs and tissues (bone marrow, thymus, lymph nodes, MALT, tonsils and spleen), their histology, and where the B and T cells live in each. He moved quickly and stopped on the points he wanted known. His slides also carry speaker notes, and the details from them that he didn't say aloud stay in these notes, marked as his slide's. These notes follow the recording and slides. His objectives: tell the blood cells apart and say what each does; know what the lymphoid organs do, which are primary or secondary, their histology, and where the B and T cells sit in each. The course objectives name the spleen and the thymus. He said twice that the exam won't test stained images: "There's not any images on your exam, necessarily," and, at the thymus, "I'm not gonna ask you any questions specifically on stained images, so you don't have to worry about those too much." So these notes describe each cell and region by its features. The cells of the blood Hematology is the study of the blood and its cells. Blood holds three kinds of cells. The erythrocytes, the red blood cells, are most of them, about 99 percent of the cells in the blood, and they carry oxygen and carbon dioxide; oxygen transport is their main job. The platelets are pieces of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow, and they initiate blood clotting: he said they play a role in the clotting cascade. "Remember, platelets arise from megakaryocytes. That's just knowledge you should know." The rest are the white blood cells, or leukocytes, and "what you need to remember with white blood cells is we've got two classes and 5 types." The granulocytes have prominent granules in their cytoplasm ("one has granules, right? Okay, don't make it hard"), and, as a hint, he said they play a role in innate immunity. They are the neutrophils, the eosinophils and the basophils. The agranulocytes don't have prominent granules: the monocytes and the lymphocytes, which come in different flavors: the B cells, T cells and NK cells. How common each white cell is follows a fixed order, and he gave each share aloud: neutrophils 50 to 70 percent, lymphocytes 30 to 40 percent, monocytes 2 to 8 percent, eosinophils 1 to 4 percent, and basophils under 1 percent. A memory cue for the order, most to least common: Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas (neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils). His summary table also gives a typical count per liter of blood for each cell. He said: "No reason to memorize the typical concentration of cells. You can, of course, review the names and functions." So learn each cell's name, share of the white count and job, not the counts per liter. Where the blood cells come from His hematopoiesis figure starts on the left with the early phase: one pluripotential stem cell, with a lot of mitotic activity, that "can become anything it wants to." It gives rise to two multipotential stem cells. The lymphoid multipotential cells migrate to the lymphoid organs, and their lymphocyte colony-forming cells become lymphoblasts and then the B and T lymphocytes. The myeloid multipotential stem cell stays in the bone marrow, and all of its lines run through colony-forming cells: one for the erythrocytes (by way of the erythroblast), one for the megakaryocytes (by way of the megakaryoblast; pieces of the megakaryocyte break off as the platelets), ones for the monocytes and for the neutrophils, and ones for the eosinophils and basophils. So a monocyte is a myeloid cell even though it has no prominent granules, and the lymphocytes are the lymphoid line. He asked the class whether lymphocytes are granulocytes or agranulocytes: agranulocytes. In an adult, every one of these cells comes from the bone marrow: the T and B lymphocytes, the mononuclear phagocytes, the platelets, the erythrocytes and the other leukocytes. Innate and adaptive immunity The cells of the immune system take part in two kinds of immunity. Nonspecific, or innate, immunity is what "your body just does": pre-existing defenses against microbial invasion, in place without any sequence of events to set them off. It has five parts: physical barriers, the skin and mucous membranes; chemical defenses, such as the low pH of some regions of the body; secretory substances, such as lysozyme, thiocyanate (in saliva) and interferons; phagocytic cells, the macrophages, neutrophils and monocytes; and the natural killer (NK) cells. Specific, or adaptive, immunity produces acquired resistance, and it takes a sequence of events. A first contact with a specific antigen starts a chain of reactions carried out by the effector B and T cells, and it often leaves a state of immune memory. It has two arms, which aren't independent: they act together. The humoral response belongs to the B cells: they make antibodies, which mark invaders for destruction by other cells. The cellular immune response belongs to the T cells: it targets transformed cells and virus-infected cells for destruction. His shortcut: "When you hear the word humoral, think B-cell response. And then also, when you hear B cells, think about the production of antibodies." Thiocyanate in saliva is the dentist's entry on his innate list. Introducing the NK cells there, he said "we'll figure out how those function as killer T cells," and his slide puts "(Killer T cells)" after them. NK cells are not T cells: at their own slide he said they "lack the B or T cell-specific markers." The killer T cells are the cytotoxic, CD8-positive T cells of adaptive immunity. Neutrophils Neutrophils are the most numerous white cells, 50 to 70 percent, the main phagocyte of the blood, and "the body's first line of defense against bacteria." They are highly motile. They last in the blood for about 10 hours, then migrate into the tissues. To recognize one by its features: a multi-lobed nucleus, not many mitochondria but a lot of glycogen, and two types of granules. The primary granules contain elastase and myeloperoxidase. The other granules, which he and his slide call azure granules, contain lysozyme and proteases. As he put it, a phagocyte eats things, then uses these enzymes to break them down. His summary table gives their job in one line: they phagocytose and destroy invading bacteria. He read the granules the way his slide labels them: "primary granules, which are going to contain elastase and myeloperoxidase, ... and azure granules, which are going to contain lysozyme and proteases." Histology texts (Junqueira, Ross) call the primary granules the azurophilic ones and the second kind the specific granules. Learn the contents: elastase and myeloperoxidase in the primary granules, lysozyme and proteases in the other kind. No question here asks which kind is azurophilic. Eosinophils Eosinophils are 1 to 4 percent of the white cells. Their features: a bilobed nucleus, which looks like two nuclei joined together, and large specific granules that stain red, or pink, with eosin, the dye they are named for. Their granules hold two weapons. Peroxidase binds to microorganisms and helps kill them. Major basic protein, MBP, also called PRG2, binds to and disrupts the membranes of parasites, both protozoa and helminths (worms), and it also makes basophils release histamine. Eosinophils respond strongly to parasites: they accumulate in the blood and tissues in parasitic infections, and their numbers rise in allergic reactions such as hay fever. They carry surface receptors for IgE, the antibody seen mainly in allergic responses. His table: they destroy larger parasites and modulate allergic responses. Basophils Basophils are the rarest white cell, under 1 percent. The nucleus is typically bilobed, and the very large granules stain dark blue or purple, so a basophil is easy to pick out in a stained smear. The granules contain heparin and vasoactive substances; his table says basophils release histamine in certain immune reactions. Basophils also carry IgE receptors. When IgE binds them, the basophil releases its vasoactive contents. Basophils play a prominent role in bronchial asthma. Eosinophils and basophils both have a bilobed nucleus and IgE receptors. Tell them apart by the granules: red with eosin (the eosinophil: peroxidase and major basic protein, parasites and allergy) or dark blue to purple (the basophil: heparin and histamine, asthma). Monocytes Monocytes are 2 to 8 percent of the white cells. They are fairly large cells with a single nucleus that, he said, doesn't look bilobed or multi-lobed; his slide calls it often indented or horseshoe-shaped, and the cells have prominent lysosomes. They circulate for about 3 days. During inflammation they migrate into the tissues, where they differentiate into macrophages; together the monocytes and macrophages make up the mononuclear phagocytic system. They phagocytose bacteria, cells and tissue debris, and they express MHC class II molecules, which is how a macrophage presents antigen to helper T cells. Lymphocytes Lymphocytes are 30 to 40 percent of the white cells. They come in two sizes: the NK cells are "pretty large," and the B and T cells "a little bit smaller." His slide gives about 9 to 12 micrometers for the large ones and about 6 to 8 for the small ones. A lymphocyte has a big, slightly indented nucleus that takes up most of the cell, so its light-staining cytoplasm is only a thin rim around it. The lymphocytes circulating in the blood are immunocompetent: they have the capacity to recognize and respond to antigens. There are three classes: B cells, T cells and NK cells. B cells mature into antibody-making plasma cells, and that happens in the secondary lymphoid organs. His slide writes the sizes in "mm"; lymphocytes are measured in micrometers, and he didn't give the numbers aloud. A monocyte's nucleus is indented too, but the monocyte is the larger cell, with more cytoplasm. B cells and the humoral response B lymphocytes carry the humoral response: "if you hear the word humoral, you're thinking B lymphocyte, you're thinking antibody production in some form or fashion." Each B cell makes and displays membrane-bound antibodies, IgM and IgD, which act as its receptors for antigens, and each mature B cell answers one antigen. His drawing showed it: a B cell whose antibody doesn't fit a star-shaped antigen can't bind it, but one whose antibody fits does. That binding generates a chemical signal that recruits helper T cells, and the B cell transforms into a plasma cell, which makes a great many antibodies like the one that bound and releases them into the circulation. Two points about plasma cells. B cells mature into plasma cells in the secondary lymphoid organs, not in the marrow. And helper T cells are essential for it: his slide says they make lymphokines, chemical signals that drive the B cell to become an antibody-secreting plasma cell. At the lymph node he came back to it: "You know that term, plasma cell. And you can associate that with antibody production and release." Twice he said "IgG" where he meant an antibody in general: B cells "can mature into IgG-producing plasma cells," and a mature B cell has "a single antigen-specific IgG that they express on their surface, like IgM or IgD." His slide notes do the same. The receptors on a B cell's surface are IgM and IgD, as he also said. IgG in its own sense comes up with the NK cell's CD16, which binds IgG's constant region. T cells and the cellular response T lymphocytes carry the cellular immune response. They don't carry antibodies on their surface. Their membrane receptor for antigen, the T cell receptor or TCR, recognizes antigen only when it is bound to MHC molecules: it has to be presented to them, on the surface of a cell such as an antigen-presenting cell or a virus-infected cell. T cells also carry immunologic memory. (CD, in CD4 and CD8, stands for cluster of differentiation.) There are two main types, and he kept their jobs simple: "the helper T cells are what's going to help our B lymphocytes, and the cytotoxic T cells are probably just gonna kill whatever they bind." They respond slightly differently, he said, but "we don't really get into it," so the details below are his slide's. Helper T cells, TH, are CD4 positive. An antigen-presenting cell such as a macrophage shows them antigen on MHC class II. When the TCR binds that antigen and MHC II complex, the helper T cell is activated: it makes interleukins that act on itself (autocrine), so more CD4 cells proliferate and differentiate, and it secretes lymphokines that drive the differentiation of B cells, T cells and NK cells. Helper T cells are critical for starting an immune response to a foreign antigen, and his slide adds that cytokines can also trigger them. Cytotoxic T cells, CTL or TC, are CD8 positive and recognize antigen on MHC class I. Once the TCR binds, they secrete lymphokines and perforins, which open ion channels in the infected cell's membrane and lyse it. They play a significant role in rejecting allografts, transplanted tissue, and in tumor immunology. Marker CD4 CD8 Reads antigen on MHC class II MHC class I Shown it by Antigen-presenting cells such as macrophages Virus-infected and other altered cells What it does Interleukins (more CD4 cells) and lymphokines that drive B, T and NK cells; B cells need it to become plasma cells Perforins open ion channels and lyse the cell; allograft rejection and tumor immunology A memory cue: CD4 times MHC 2 makes 8, and CD8 times MHC 1 makes 8. CD4 goes with MHC II, CD8 with MHC I. NK cells and ADCC Natural killer cells, NK cells, are the large lymphocytes. They lack the B and T cell markers and lack specific antigen receptors. What they do is recognize altered cells, such as tumor cells and virus-infected cells. Their surface markers include CD16, CD56 and CD94. CD16 is an Fc receptor: it binds the constant region of IgG, which is how NK cells take part in antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity, ADCC: it needs an antibody, and it ends in killing the cell the antibody marks. NK cells mature in the bone marrow, and they belong to innate immunity. In ADCC, circulating antibodies bind the antigens on a target cell's surface. The Fc receptors on NK cells, macrophages, neutrophils and eosinophils then bind the antibody-coated target, and the killer cell secretes lytic enzymes, perforins, TNF and granzymes (his slide's list), which together kill the target. The antibody picks the target and the killer cell does the killing, with no T cell receptor and no MHC involved. His ADCC picture puts a target cell in the middle with an NK cell, a neutrophil, an eosinophil and a macrophage around it: he had presented them one by one, but "they all play a role in concert together." How an NK cell decides to kill He called his NK schematic "pretty helpful": it shows what an NK cell does in three scenarios. The NK cell carries two receptors: an activating receptor, which binds an activating ligand on the other cell, and an inhibitory receptor, which binds MHC class I. A healthy cell shows both the activating ligand and MHC class I. The activating receptor wants to bind the ligand, but the inhibitory receptor binds the MHC class I and stops that response: no killing. A target cell, such as a tumor cell or a virus-infected cell, still has the activating ligand but is missing its MHC class I, the signal that says "cut it out." The activating receptor binds the ligand, and the NK cell kills the target. Induced killing: the cell has both, but many more activating ligands than usual, and the NK cell kills it anyway. That is killing of the body's own cells, which is not good: he said it is probably playing a role in autoimmune responses. Once, describing the target cell, he said it was missing "MHC class 2"; a moment before, he twice said the inhibitory receptor binds MHC class 1, and his schematic and immunology texts agree. NK cells check for MHC class I. What the lymphoid organs do The lymphoid, or immune, system protects the body from pathogens, foreign substances and abnormal cells. Its organs mainly detect and inactivate foreign substances: invading microorganisms, foreign materials, the cells of transplanted organs and cancer cells. Lymph, in the lymphatic system, also brings nutrients from the blood vessels to the cells and picks up their waste. The lymphoid organs supply the immunocompetent cells that react with and neutralize antigens, and they tell self from non-self. Lymphoid tissue is lymphocytes and mononuclear phagocytes held in a framework of reticular cells and fibers, a specialized reticular connective tissue. It comes in several arrangements. The most widespread is diffuse lymphocytes under the epithelium of the GI, respiratory and genitourinary tracts, the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, MALT. Denser spherical clusters are nodules, or follicles, single or in permanent groups such as the tonsils and Peyer's patches. Then come the discrete organs: the encapsulated lymph nodes, spleen and thymus, and the unencapsulated bone marrow. The organs are classed as primary or secondary. His overview figure shows the primary organs in yellow and the secondary ones in pink. "You don't have to memorize this huge list," he said; "we'll talk about what they're doing." The figure lists GALT among the primary organs, and he struck it: "We're not going to consider GALT as a primary lymphatic organ, but we will consider the thymus and the bone marrow as our primary lymphoid organs." The primary lymphoid organs are the main sites where lymphocytes are made and mature: the bone marrow, where B cells develop, and the thymus, where T cells mature. "If you know those two are primary and we're talking about any other lymphoid organ, then you know it's secondary": the immune responses themselves happen in the secondary lymphoid organs, the lymph nodes, MALT with its gut-associated part, GALT, and the spleen. The stroma Every lymphoid organ's cells sit in a stroma, an internal framework of cells, and the blood that flows into the organ passes through it, where it meets many cells and can set off many reactions. In every lymphoid organ except the thymus, the stroma is reticular cells and reticulin fibers, which are type III collagen. The thymus is the exception: its stroma is the cell processes of the epithelioreticular cells. "I do want you to know that. So epithelioreticular cells, you should associate that with the thymus." Here he said reticulin is "a type 2 collagen fiber"; at the lymph node he said the reticular cells secrete "type 3 collagen," which is what his slides and histology texts say. Reticulin is type III collagen. The slide he used for this was a spleen section, and he said "there's a lot more information than you need to know on the periphery here": its point is the stroma. Primary lymphoid organs: the bone marrow As an overview, he said, "the bone marrow is gonna serve as our B-cell development center, the thymus is gonna serve as our T-cell center." (A medical student on the stairs before an immunology test got the same answer from him: "bone marrow, B cells, thymus, T cells.") Both organs turn lymphocytes into mature, immunocompetent cells. The thymus is where naive T cells develop, where the T cell receptor genes are rearranged, and where T cells are selected. His slide also names the liver in the fetus as a B cell development zone, but for this class the primary organs are the bone marrow and the thymus. In the marrow, the stromal cells interact with the B cells and make the cytokines that govern B cell development, and the B cells gain their antigen specificity there. Self-reactive B cells are eliminated in the bone marrow: "we really don't want a B cell that goes out into the tissue" and treats normal tissue as something to destroy. The B cells that leave are immunocompetent: each displays a single antigen-specific antibody, IgM or IgD, on its surface, and they travel to the secondary lymphoid organs. His slide also names the colony-forming units here (the lymphoid CFU-Ly splitting into CFU-LyB for the B cells and CFU-LyT for the T cells); he said you don't have to worry about that sentence, since the opening hematopoiesis figure covers what each line gives rise to. Three lymphocytes, two homes. B cells and NK cells both form and mature in the bone marrow, then enter the blood and populate the secondary lymphoid organs, the epithelia and the connective tissue. T cell precursors also originate in the marrow, but they leave it immunoincompetent, negative for both CD4 and CD8, travel to the thymus and mature there, and leave it as CD4-positive or CD8-positive cells. The thymus The thymus is the site of T cell maturation, and the T cells inside it are called thymocytes. It is a flattened, bilobed organ that lies behind the manubrium of the sternum and extends into the mediastinum (his slide: the superior and anterior mediastinum). It is very large when you are born and little: largest and most active in the newborn and before adolescence, about 12 to 15 grams at birth and 30 to 40 grams by puberty (his slide's numbers). By the time you are a teenager, or a little past then, it shrinks, which is thymic involution, and fat replaces it. He said that in a donor you see a lot of fat in front of the heart: that is where the old thymus was. It comes from two germ layers. The endoderm of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches gives the epithelioreticular cells that form its stroma, and the mesoderm gives the mesenchyme that forms its capsule and trabeculae. The capsule and trabeculae carry blood vessels, nerves and efferent, but not afferent, lymphatic vessels. The trabeculae divide the thymus into thymic lobules, each with an outer cortex and an inner medulla. Inside it, the T cells get their antigenic diversity (their receptor genes are rearranged), and a great many cells die during thymocyte selection: about 95 to 99 percent of the cells that go there are selected out and die by apoptosis. The thymic cortex and medulla His thymus section shows an outer capsule, with blood vessels following it, around the cortex, and the medulla in the middle. The cortex is packed with developing T cells, mostly small lymphocytes, so densely that they hide the epithelioreticular cells between them, and it stains darker. The epithelioreticular cells give the developing T cells their framework, and macrophages in the cortex phagocytose the T cells that "do not go to school": the ones that fail their thymic education. Cortical lymphocytes divide often, then move into the medulla as they mature. The medulla is the inner part of the lobule. It has more epithelioreticular cells, with pale nuclei, and loosely packed T cells, and it stains lighter because its T cells are bigger and less crowded. His slide adds its distinguishing feature, the Hassall's corpuscles: concentric layers of flattened epithelial cells that stain acidophilic (pink). Macrophages and dendritic cells are found in both regions. Mature T cells leave for the T cell areas of the other lymphoid tissues: the paracortex of the lymph nodes, the periarteriolar lymphatic sheaths of the spleen, and the interfollicular regions of the Peyer's patches. The blood-thymus barrier The blood-thymus barrier has three layers, which he listed from the outside in: an epithelioreticular cell layer, a perivascular connective tissue layer (with macrophages in it, his slide adds), and the capillary wall, the endothelium and its basement membrane. The two outer layers surround the capillary wall. The barrier protects the developing T cells from antigens in the bloodstream: "we don't really want to expose these T cells too much and make them hyperactive." It also keeps them apart from the mature lymphocytes circulating in the blood. The perivascular connective tissue sits between the endothelium's basal lamina and the epithelioreticular cells' basal lamina. Histology texts place the barrier around the capillaries of the cortex, where the developing thymocytes are. Thymic education Thymic education turns the immunoincompetent precursors into immunocompetent T cells. The precursors enter the medulla through postcapillary venules as immunoincompetent cells ("they don't have any education") and migrate to the cortex, at the edge of the lobule. Their T cell receptors develop as they migrate and meet self antigens. His slide tracks the CD markers they gain and lose: CD2 and CD7 mark an early stage and CD1 a middle one; as they mature they express the T cell receptor, CD3, and both CD4 and CD8. Then come positive and negative selection, which most of the cells fail; his slide puts them in order. In the cortex, the epithelioreticular cells present antigen on MHC molecules: a thymocyte whose receptor recognizes them survives, and one that doesn't dies. This is positive selection. The survivors move into the medulla for negative selection, which eliminates the cells aimed at self antigen displayed on self MHC. The cells that pass both become CD8-positive cytotoxic or CD4-positive helper T cells, ready for an immune response, and they leave through postcapillary venules into the circulation and migrate to the secondary lymphoid organs. His notes phrase positive selection as a thymocyte recognizing "self or foreign" antigen; textbooks put it as recognizing self MHC. Either way, the order is the point: positive selection in the cortex, negative selection in the medulla, and single-positive cells leaving. The primary organs in summary The primary lymphoid organs, just the bone marrow and the thymus "for our class," develop immunocompetent B and T cells in the absence of antigen. The blood and lymph carry those cells to the secondary lymphoid organs, and B and T cells are activated by antigen in the secondary, or peripheral, organs. Secondary lymphoid organs He narrowed the long list: "Really, what we want to remember is lymph nodes, MALT and GALT, and spleen. We'll look at the tonsils as well." The activation of B and T cells takes place in these peripheral, or secondary, organs: the cells originate in the primary organs, the self-reactive ones are removed, and the rest are sent out to be further educated and made into what they need to be. The secondary organs capture antigens and give lymphocytes a place to undergo clonal proliferation and differentiate into effector cells in the presence of those antigens. Each has its own job: the lymph nodes filter lymph; MALT and GALT, sitting with the epithelia, are the first defense against external antigens; and the spleen filters blood. They range from loose to highly organized: diffuse collections of lymphocytes and macrophages, as in MALT and GALT; lymphoid follicles, which are aggregates of lymphoid cells, stromal cells and macrophages surrounded by lymphatic capillaries; the lymph nodes, with several follicles and distinct regions of B and T cell activity; and the spleen, also with distinct B and T cell regions. Lymphatic vessels Lymphatic vessels begin as networks of blind-ended capillaries in loose connective tissue. They remove fluid and substances from the tissue spaces, and once a substance enters them it is called lymph. The lymph collects into lymphatic vessels and makes its way to a lymph node, where the antigens are trapped and presented by antigen-presenting cells to the cells that came from the primary organs. His slide adds the build: the walls are permeable, so large molecules, antigens and cells get in, and lymphatic capillaries are built like blood capillaries but lack a basal lamina; small anchoring filaments tie their endothelial cells to nearby collagen fibers and keep them from collapsing. Like veins, lymphatic vessels have valves and thin walls, and the contraction of the muscles around them moves the lymph along. The vessels join to form the thoracic duct, and the large lymphatic vessels drain into the subclavian veins. Lymph nodes Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped, encapsulated organs along the lymphatic vessels: some very small, some big enough to see, as the class saw in the head and neck. His slide puts 500 to 600 of them in places such as the neck, groin and axillae. They serve as filters, with one-way valves, an entry point and an exit point: whatever gets into the node circulates around and has time to react. During development each node's regions are seeded with B cells from the bone marrow and T cells from the thymus. His slide and its speaker notes give different size ranges for a lymph node, and he gave none aloud, so there is no number to learn here. Their jobs: filtering the lymph before it returns to the thoracic duct; producing lymphocytes that are added to the lymph; making antibodies, mostly IgG; and recirculating lymphocytes. A dense fibrous capsule surrounds each node and sends trabeculae of collagen inward, which support it and carry its blood vessels. Between them, a stroma of reticular fibers holds the lymphocytes, along with reticular cells, fixed macrophages and dendritic cells. A node has three regions. The outer cortex, just under the capsule, is made of lymphoid nodules of B cells from the bone marrow. The paracortex, the deep cortex, holds the T cells. The inner part is the medulla. The cortex has two kinds of nodules, or follicles, and he pointed out both in a stained node. A primary, unstimulated follicle is a spherical aggregate of B cells in a meshwork of reticular fibers. After antigenic stimulation it becomes a secondary, stimulated follicle, with a germinal center surrounded by a mantle zone. The germinal center is the major site of B cell proliferation, holding small and large lymphocytes, lymphoblasts and follicular dendritic cells; the mantle holds small lymphocytes. Meanwhile, antigen-dependent T cell differentiation and proliferation happen in the paracortex. The supporting cells of a lymph node Reticular cells make and secrete the type III collagen and the matrix that form the stroma, the internal part of the organ. Dendritic cells look the way the name sounds, with many tentacle-like processes. They are antigen-presenting cells: they watch for foreign particles and present them to T cells. Macrophages are phagocytic and also present antigen; there are fewer of them than dendritic cells. Follicular dendritic cells have many thin, hair-like processes that interdigitate between the B cells of the germinal centers. Antigen-antibody complexes stick to those processes through Fc receptors. His slide adds that follicular dendritic cells are not antigen-presenting cells, because they lack MHC II molecules. Two cells with "dendritic" in the name: the dendritic cell presents antigen to T cells; the follicular dendritic cell holds antigen-antibody complexes among the B cells of a germinal center and presents nothing. How lymph and lymphocytes move through a node His schematic follows the lymph. An afferent lymphatic vessel, with valves that direct the flow, brings lymph from the surrounding tissues into the subcapsular sinus, just under the capsule. From there it runs into the trabecular sinuses, beside the trabeculae, with the chance to pass through a germinal center on the way, and it leaves in the efferent lymphatic vessel. Around the sinuses are the outer cortex, with its superficial and deep layers, and the inner medulla, and blood comes into the node too, through its own capillaries. His slide adds how the filtering works: the sinus walls let the lymph percolate into the superficial and deep cortex, where the lymphocytes carry out immunosurveillance, and macrophages reach into the sinuses and phagocytose antigens and foreign material. Lymphocytes also arrive from the blood. Blood comes in through an artery at the hilum, and its lymphocytes cross into the deep cortex through the high endothelial venules, HEVs. T cells and dendritic cells are directed to the paracortex, and B cells to the cortex. Both leave the node through the efferent lymphatic vessel. The lymph node is the only lymphoid structure with both afferent and efferent lymphatics. Then he walked an antigen through the node, region by region: The antigen comes in through the afferent lymphatic vessel. In the paracortex: the initial T and B cell activation. In a primary follicle: B cell activation. In the germinal center of a secondary follicle: B cell proliferation and differentiation. In the medulla: plasma cells secrete antibody. Out through the efferent lymphatic vessel. His slide adds that the antigen arrives carried by dendritic cells or in soluble form, and that plasma cells release their antibody into the lymph. Put it to work in the clinic: a tender, swollen node under the jaw after a tooth infection is this process. Antigen from the infected area arrives in the afferent lymph, and B cells multiply in new germinal centers in the cortex. MALT, GALT and the Peyer's patches The linings of the GI, respiratory and genitourinary tracts face the outside world and its microbes. The diffuse lymphoid tissue in the lamina propria of these membranes is MALT, named by where it is: gut-associated (GALT), bronchus-associated (BALT), nasal-associated (NALT) and vulvovaginal-associated (VALT). GALT includes the tonsils, the Peyer's patches, the appendix, and looser collections of lymphocytes along the GI tract. MALT is lymphocytes on a loose framework of reticular fibers, with nodules: dense, spherical, unencapsulated clusters. A primary nodule holds small immature B cells; after antigen exposure it becomes a secondary nodule with a germinal center, where B cells proliferate and differentiate into plasma cells. The main antibody MALT makes is IgA, which is actively transported into the mucosal lumen. MALT has both B and T cells: B cells dominate the nodules, and T cells are plentiful in the areas around them. Peyer's patches are in the ileum: aggregations of lymphoid nodules in its wall, dark purple in a stained section. M cells, which he reached back to histology for, are the epithelial cells that cover the Peyer's patches, and they are antigen-transporting cells. They take up microorganisms and macromolecules from the lumen (in endocytic vesicles, his slide says), carry them to their basolateral membrane, and release them near the B cells and CD4-positive T cells, which turns them into an immune reaction and sends B and T cells out into the circulation. Macrophages under the epithelium also process the material and present it. The tonsils and Waldeyer's ring The tonsils are aggregates of lymphoid tissue under the epithelium at the entrances to the digestive and respiratory tracts, and they are part of MALT. He walked through them on a sagittal section of the head: the pharyngeal tonsil, in the back of the nasal cavity (the nasopharynx); the tubal tonsils, at the torus tubarius, where the auditory tube opens; the palatine tonsils, a pair in the back of the throat, which you can see if you still have them (many people have them removed); the lingual tonsils, on the back of the tongue, which is why it looks rough. Together they form Waldeyer's ring, a broken circle of lymphoid tissue around the entrance to the nasopharynx and oropharynx. They sit where you breathe, eat and drink all day, so they start the response early: if you just ate a salmonella chicken sandwich, he said, it doesn't stop you from getting sick, but it starts to mount the response. The palatine tonsils have tonsillar crypts, where substances get wedged in, which gives the tissue a longer time to respond. His slide adds that the tonsils have no afferent lymphatic vessels, only efferent ones. Their main job is defense against bacterial and viral infections, through the immunoglobulins made by plasma cells that come from their B cells. In children, the pharyngeal tonsil commonly enlarges and stays inflamed. That is adenoiditis, and it can obstruct breathing. The pharyngeal tonsil is what patients call the adenoid. A child whose enlarged adenoid blocks the nose breathes through the mouth, which you will see in the chair. The spleen The spleen, a secondary lymphoid organ, filters blood and responds to systemic, blood-borne infections. It lies in the upper left quadrant of the abdomen, behind the stomach and just below the diaphragm. In adults it is the largest lymphoid organ, about the size of a clenched fist. At its hilum, the large splenic artery, a branch of the celiac trunk, enters with the nerves, and it carries the blood-borne antigens and lymphocytes into the spleen. The splenic vein and lymphatics leave there. It has no afferent lymphatics; its efferent lymphatics leave at the hilum. What the spleen does: Filters the blood, clearing particulate matter, infectious microorganisms, and aged and defective red cells and platelets Recycles iron from the red cells Stores about a third of the body's platelets Holds a large share of the mononuclear phagocytes, and of the body's lymphocytes (his notes say about a quarter) Its lymphocytes respond to blood-borne antigens, activating T and B cells, and it produces lymphocytes, plasma cells, and both IgM and IgG In the fetus, it is also an organ of hematopoiesis, before the bone marrow takes over The spleen has a very dense capsule of connective tissue, which sends trabeculae, containing myofibroblasts, into the organ. Between the trabeculae is a network of reticular fibers with macrophages and reticular cells attached. The spleen's parenchyma is the splenic pulp, and it comes in two kinds: white pulp and red pulp, named for their colors in the fresh spleen. He said the spleen looks the way you'd expect lymphoid tissue to look, with a capsule, trabeculae, "the cortex, and ... kind of a medulla area." His slide notes and histology texts say the spleen has no true cortex and medulla: its tissue is white pulp and red pulp, with the white pulp in islands through the red pulp. Learn it as white pulp and red pulp; no question here turns on whether it has a cortex. White pulp and red pulp The white pulp is islands of lymphoid tissue around a central arteriole (he called it the central artery), which comes from the splenic artery after many treelike branchings. In it he pointed out a primary follicle, a marginal zone, germinal centers and the PALS, the periarteriolar lymphatic sheath: the lymphocytes wrapped around the arteriole ("peri means around"), which "I'll just say is associated with the T-cell area." "The main thing is just to really associate this PALS with the spleen," he said, and at the end: "If you see a central artery, that's where you have that area of PALS." Lymphoid nodules lie farther out in the white pulp, and they are the B cells: primary nodules, or secondary ones with germinal centers, as in the lymph nodes. A nodule pushes the arteriole off to one side. Around the white pulp is a shell of sparsely cellular lymphoid tissue, the marginal zone, with macrophages and some B cells (his slide). The red pulp makes up most of the spleen, and its color comes from its many red cells. It is thin-walled venous sinusoids, the splenic sinuses, with the splenic cords, the cords of Billroth, between them. The cords are spaces between the sinuses with a scaffold of reticular fibers, holding reticular cells, lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages and all the formed elements of the blood. Blood flow through the spleen He traced the start of it: the trabecular artery comes into the white pulp, where the sinuses at the perimeter are the marginal sinuses; it continues into the red pulp and branches into penicillar arterioles, which cross toward the venous side. Then: "You can kind of read through this. The main thing is just to really associate this PALS with the spleen." The rest of this section is his slide's. The splenic artery enters at the hilum and divides into trabecular arteries, which branch and enter the white pulp as the central arterioles, with two layers of smooth muscle and the cuff of lymphocytes that forms the PALS. Some branches of a central arteriole end in marginal sinuses at the edge of the white pulp, supplying the marginal zone. Others continue into the red pulp as short, straight penicillar arterioles, which drain into sheathed capillaries, wrapped in a sheath of reticular fibers and many macrophages. In the open circulation, the sheathed capillaries empty directly into the reticular meshwork of the splenic cords rather than connecting to the endothelium-lined sinuses. The blood seeps slowly between the cords, where macrophages sample it, then reenters the circulation through the splenic sinuses. In the closed route, capillaries drain straight into the sinuses. Two slide slips, neither one taken up aloud. His circulation slide puts "(PALS)" after the sheathed capillaries, but the PALS is the T cell sheath around the central arteriole in the white pulp, which is where he put it aloud; the sheathed capillaries are wrapped in macrophages, in the red pulp. And the slide teaches the open route, while his notes on the next slide say about 90 percent of red pulp capillaries drain straight into the sinuses; he didn't mention open or closed circulation. Know what each route is; no question here turns on which one is more common. The splenic sinuses The splenic sinuses are special sinusoidal vessels. They are lined by rod-shaped, loosely packed endothelial cells that run lengthwise, with slit-like spaces between them, and macrophage processes reach between the cells to monitor the passing blood for foreign antigens. They have only strands of basal lamina, which loop around the endothelial cells at right angles, like the hoops around the staves of a leaky barrel. They have no smooth muscle and no pericytes. Blood cells move across the wall by squeezing through the slits (his slide). The sinuses drain into larger venules, then the trabecular veins, which merge into the splenic vein that leaves at the hilum. He ended on a stained spleen: a trabecula cut across looks like a circle, the red pulp stands out from the white pulp, and in the red pulp the pulp cords and splenic sinuses are where the fluid in the spleen gets trapped and sits long enough for a reaction. Where the B and T cells are Bone marrow Form and mature (with the NK cells); self-reactive ones eliminated Precursors arise, then leave immunoincompetent Thymus Not its job Mature: dense in the cortex, then the medulla Lymph node Cortex: the follicles and their germinal centers Paracortex (deep cortex) Spleen White pulp nodules; some in the marginal zone PALS around the central arteriole MALT, Peyer's patches The nodules The areas around them (interfollicular regions) If a question describes a region instead of naming it, find the landmark: a central arteriole means the spleen's white pulp, Hassall's corpuscles mean the thymic medulla, high endothelial venules mean the lymph node paracortex, and a germinal center means B cells.
